title: Is Oracle Stock Underperforming the S&P 500?
detail:
Is Oracle Stock Underperforming the S&P 500?
Kritika Sarmah
Sat, August 29, 2026 at 11:44 AM CDT 2 min read
ORCL
^GSPC
Trade Oracle on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Austin, Texas-based Oracle Corporation (ORCL) is a global technology company specializing in enterprise software, databases, and cloud computing. Valued at a market cap of $434.5 billion, Oracle has built its business around its widely used database technology, while increasingly shifting its focus toward cloud infrastructure and AI-powered enterprise applications.

Companies with a market capitalization of $200 billion or more are typically referred to as "mega-cap stocks." ORCL fits right into that category, with its market cap exceeding this threshold, reflecting its substantial size and influence in the software infrastructure industry.

However, the stock currently trades 56.4% below its 52-week high of $345.72 recorded on Sep. 10, 2025. ORCL has declined 26% over the past three months, notably outperforming the S&P 500 Index ($SPX), which has rallied 2%. 

www.barchart.com

The stock fell 37.2% over the past 52 weeks and 22.6% on a YTD basis, underperforming the index's 18.6% rise and 12.7% rally over the same time frames. 

ORCL has been trading below its 200-day moving average since mid-June and has recently climbed above its 50-day moving average. 

www.barchart.com

Oracle has underperformed the broader market over the past year largely because investors have become increasingly concerned that the enormous cost of its AI infrastructure expansion could outweigh the near-term benefits of its strong cloud growth. Oracle raised $43 billion of debt in FY2026 and expects to raise roughly another $40 billion in FY2027, including a planned $20 billion equity issuance, to finance its AI data-center buildout. This has raised concerns about higher leverage, potential shareholder dilution and weaker free cash flow,

Compared with its rival, Palantir Technologies Inc. (PLTR) has grown 17.8% over the past year and 4.8% in 2026, outperforming ORCL.

Wall Street continues to favor the stock highly. Among the 44 analysts tracking ORCL, the overall consensus stands at a "Strong Buy." Its mean price target of $251.50 suggests 66.7% upside potential from current price levels.

Has Microsoft Stock Run Ahead Of Its AI Payoff?
Trefis Team

Image by Pexels from Pixabay

The software giant's stock has a powerful business engine behind its long-term trend, but a rapid run-up back toward all-time highs forces investors to ask if the price of admission is still worth paying.

Microsoft (MSFT) has built one of the most durable cash-generation engines in enterprise technology, but its stock currently trades about 6% below its 52-week high. For any investor sizing up the company's dominant push into artificial intelligence, the central question is clear: is this a consolidation pause before another leg higher, or has the current price already captured the payoff? While the stock's broader trend strength ranks near the middle of US-listed stocks above $1B, the recent rally to within 6% of its 52-week high brings the core tension into focus: does the fundamental engine justify the elevated valuation?

The core investment case rests on this underlying operational momentum rather than technical strength, raising the question of whether the current price offers sufficient upside for new buyers.

Is This a Genuine Business Surge?

The numbers behind Microsoft's run are strong. The company's operating margin over the last twelve months is a huge 47%, far outpacing the S&P 500 median of 18.5%. This isn't a one-time event; its three-year average is similarly high. Revenue growth tells the same story, at 17.8% over the past year, more than double the 8.3% median for the index.

This financial power comes directly from its strategic execution in AI and cloud computing. In its most recent quarter, revenue from Azure and other cloud services grew 43%, a clear sign that demand for its AI services is intense. Management confirmed that "Customer demand continues to exceed available capacity." The adoption of its AI tools is also rapid, with the company reporting it now has "over 30 million paid Microsoft 365 Copilot seats."

What Does a Share of This Engine Cost?

The market is well aware of this operational strength, and it charges a premium. Microsoft trades at a price-to-earnings multiple of 28.0, compared to an S&P 500 median of 23.3. That premium exists even after a stretch of relative underperformance: over the trailing twelve months, Microsoft has been largely flat, trailing the S&P 500's +21% return. The stock also trades about 6% below its two-year high of $537.65, reinforcing that buyers today are not chasing a fresh peak.

The primary risk centers on the sheer scale of capital expenditure required to sustain this AI buildout. Some analysts are asking if soaring capital expenditures could put the stock's valuation at risk. The concern is that the company is building for a level of demand that might not materialize, or that rising component costs could squeeze profitability. This risk is compounded by declines in legacy businesses. Management expects revenue from its Windows OEM and Devices segment to "decline in the high teens for the fiscal year," and Xbox revenue recently decreased 10%. For investors who prefer broader exposure to the technology sector without concentrating on a single company's execution risk, a technology ETF like VGT might be an alternative.

title: Is Oracle Stock Getting Too Cheap To Ignore After A 53% Drop?

Image from Pixabay

For Oracle stock, the upside now depends less on the size of the order book than on the pace at which the company can energize what it has already sold.

Oracle (ORCL) has spent the past year getting cheaper while its order book got bigger. The stock is down about 34% over the trailing twelve months and sits roughly 53% below its high of the past year, at a market value of about $436.8 billion, even as contracted future work reached $638 billion.

Just 12% Of The Backlog Is Expected To Reach Revenue Inside A Year

Remaining performance obligations finished fiscal 2026 at $638 billion, up from $553 billion at the end of fiscal Q3 2026. Management expects 12% of that to convert within twelve months, roughly $77 billion, against $67.4 billion of revenue over the trailing twelve months, and sees that share accelerating over the coming quarters. Oracle earns that trailing-twelve-month revenue at an operating margin of 33.3%, its own three-year peak, so what comes next starts from strength rather than repair. Demand is not the constraint; a contract pays only once a data hall is energized and handed to the customer.

Oracle Guides One Quarter To Nearly Match What Fiscal 2026 Delivered In Four

Oracle handed customers more than 1.2 gigawatts across fiscal 2026, and more than 400 megawatts of that landed in fiscal Q3 2026. Management said in June that fiscal Q1 2027 delivery was approaching a gigawatt on its own, close to the previous four quarters combined. At Abilene, Texas, the company had delivered 42% of total capacity as of June, with a further 35% then due inside ninety days. In Shackelford County, Texas, first power came online ahead of schedule. Owning the shares is primarily dependent on one company's build-out arriving on time, a different proposition from the Trefis High Quality Portfolio, whose returns do not rest on the handful of largest technology names.

The Customers Are Pre-Funding Part Of The Build

What matters is the shape of the $67 billion of AI infrastructure contracts signed in fiscal Q4 2026: the majority were either bring your own hardware or prepaid, taking Oracle's cumulative pool of such contracts to $75 billion, which management says carries no margin degradation against its other contracts. The customers most eager for capacity help fund the plant that serves them, lowering the cash Oracle itself must raise. Fiscal 2027 still calls for about $70 billion of net cash capital spending, a figure already net of $20 billion to $25 billion of customer prepayments and timing. Funding it takes around $40 billion of debt and equity, including a $20 billion at-the-market issuance already announced.

A creative software titan is trading at a steep discount, but a major strategy shift has investors wondering if the price is a bargain or a breakdown.

Adobe (ADBE) is the architecture of the modern creative and business world, the company behind Photoshop, Premiere, and the ubiquitous PDF. Yet the market has put a surprisingly low price on this franchise. After a significant markdown, the stock trades at a price-to-earnings multiple of 16.1, a steep discount to the S&P 500 median of 23.3. That kind of gap on a household name forces a question every bargain hunter must answer: is this discount a buying opportunity, or does it reflect market skepticism over slowing growth?

How can a business this profitable be this cheap?

By the numbers, Adobe looks less like a company in trouble and more like a fortress. Its operating margin over the last twelve months was 36%, nearly double the S&P 500 median of 18.5%. This isn't a stagnant business, either; revenue grew 11.5% over the same period, outpacing the broader market.

More importantly, the earnings are backed by cash, and lots of it. The company's operating cash flow margin is a huge 42%, a clear sign of a high-quality, capital-light business model. The fundamentals paint a picture of a dominant enterprise that converts a huge portion of its sales directly into cash. This is the core of the value argument: a highly profitable, growing, cash-generating leader trading well below the market average.

Is a strategic pivot the real reason for the discount?

The value-trap screen found just one flaw: operating margin shrank by a slight 0.3 percentage points over the last year. But the market's real anxiety isn't about that sliver of margin; it's about a deliberate, high-stakes pivot in strategy. Management recently announced a plan to aggressively pursue a "freemium" model for its AI-powered products like Firefly, prioritizing user acquisition over immediate sales. This shift comes at a cost.

Management stated the move "lowers our second half ARR growth expectations from individual subscribers" and involves a decision to "defer previously planned Creative Cloud second half line optimizations." In short, Adobe is trading predictable, high-margin revenue for a long-term bet on converting a large new user base. This strategic gamble is happening during a leadership transition, with an active CEO search underway and an interim CFO in place, adding a layer of execution risk. An investor might wonder what the market's discount is really pricing in, given these moving parts. For those who prefer to invest in the sector as a whole, a broader software ETF like IGV offers an alternative to single-stock risk.

title: Wall Street Analysts Think Oracle (ORCL) Is a Good Investment: Is It?
detail:
Wall Street Analysts Think Oracle (ORCL) Is a Good Investment: Is It?
Zacks Equity Research
Fri, August 28, 2026 at 8:30 AM CDT 4 min read
ORCL
Trade Oracle on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Investors often turn to recommendations made by Wall Street analysts before making a Buy, Sell, or Hold decision about a stock. While media reports about rating changes by these brokerage-firm employed (or sell-side) analysts often affect a stock's price, do they really matter?

Before we discuss the reliability of brokerage recommendations and how to use them to your advantage, let's see what these Wall Street heavyweights think about Oracle (ORCL).

Oracle currently has an average brokerage recommendation (ABR) of 1.51, on a scale of 1 to 5 (Strong Buy to Strong Sell), calculated based on the actual recommendations (Buy, Hold, Sell, etc.) made by 45 brokerage firms. An ABR of 1.51 approximates between Strong Buy and Buy.

Of the 45 recommendations that derive the current ABR, 34 are Strong Buy and one is Buy. Strong Buy and Buy respectively account for 75.6% and 2.2% of all recommendations.

Brokerage Recommendation Trends for ORCL
Broker Rating Breakdown Chart for ORCL

Check price target & stock forecast for Oracle here>>>

The ABR suggests buying Oracle, but making an investment decision solely on the basis of this information might not be a good idea. According to several studies, brokerage recommendations have little to no success guiding investors to choose stocks with the most potential for price appreciation.

Are you wondering why? The vested interest of brokerage firms in a stock they cover often results in a strong positive bias of their analysts in rating it. Our research shows that for every "Strong Sell" recommendation, brokerage firms assign five "Strong Buy" recommendations.

In other words, their interests aren't always aligned with retail investors, rarely indicating where the price of a stock could actually be heading. Therefore, the best use of this information could be validating your own research or an indicator that has proven to be highly successful in predicting a stock's price movement.

Zacks Rank, our proprietary stock rating tool with an impressive externally audited track record, categorizes stocks into five groups, ranging from Zacks Rank #1 (Strong Buy) to Zacks Rank #5 (Strong Sell), and is an effective indicator of a stock's price performance in the near future. Therefore, using the ABR to validate the Zacks Rank could be an efficient way of making a profitable investment decision.

ABR Should Not Be Confused With Zacks Rank

In spite of the fact that Zacks Rank and ABR both appear on a scale from 1 to 5, they are two completely different measures.

Broker recommendations are the sole basis for calculating the ABR, which is typically displayed in decimals (such as 1.28). The Zacks Rank, on the other hand, is a quantitative model designed to harness the power of earnings estimate revisions. It is displayed in whole numbers -- 1 to 5.
